title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service recorded conversations without explicit consent from all participants, then used those recordings to train its AI systems. The company operated a system where recordings happened by default on video platforms, with the operator claiming permission came through a checkbox in its privacy policy. The lawsuit alleges that users were deceived about the scope of recording and that consent was not properly obtained from all meeting participants.

The failure point was in the deployment decision to enable recording without requiring affirmative consent from every person in a conversation. A review of consent practices before launch, particularly one that verified whether all participants understood and agreed to recording and model training, would have surfaced this discrepancy. It is not established whether users actually saw or understood the privacy policy checkbox, or what specific language appeared there.

The case remains in early stages. A court has allowed privacy claims to proceed, but no findings have been made against the company.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service used for virtual meetings, of secretly recording private work conversations without proper consent. The suit claims the company records meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without asking all participants for permission, then uses those recordings to train its AI systems. Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, California filed the class-action lawsuit alleging his privacy was violated when he discovered Otter was secretly recording a confidential conversation. The company claims users give permission through a checkbox in its privacy policy, but the lawsuit maintains many people are being deceived.

The lawsuit raises concerns about Otter's ability to properly anonymize data before feeding it into its machine learning systems. About 25 million people currently use Otter's tools, which have recorded and processed over 1 billion meetings since 2016. Recent incidents include an AI researcher discovering the company shared confidential business details that ended up killing a deal, and a journalist raising concerns about data potentially being accessible to foreign governments. Otter denies sharing data with foreign governments or law enforcement. Neither the plaintiff's legal team nor Otter responded to requests for comment.
